title: COMPOTE: Collapse-Resistant Multiple-Hypothesis Learning for Sequential Recommendation

paper.title: COMPOTE: Collapse-Resistant Multiple-Hypothesis Learning for Sequential Recommendation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Next-item prediction is inherently ambiguous: a single interaction history often admits
multiple plausible continuations across distinct catalogue regions.
Standard sequential recommenders compress these alternatives into a single prediction,
conflating user intents. We introduce CO llapse-resistant M ultiple hy POT hesis l E arning (COMPOTE),
a multi-hypothesis transformer trained with an annealed objective that transitions
from uniform supervision to a winner-takes-all assignment. This mechanism forces
hypotheses to specialize into distinct catalogue regions, while inference
relies on an efficient, normalizer-free max-similarity rule.
Theoretically, we show that in the population case, the optimal solutionspartition the conditional
next-item distribution according to a max-entropy quantization principle,
while pooled scores preserve the Bayes-optimal ranking.
We also prove a generalization bound scaling logarithmically with the number of hypotheses.
Across three Amazon Reviews 2023 benchmarks, COMPOTE outperforms strong ID-based, generative,
and multi-interest baselines using item IDs alone. Matched-capacity ablations
confirm that performance gains stem directly from the annealed
objective, preventing the head collapse observed in conventional
multi-head architectures, rather than added capacity, ensembling, or routing.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recommender systems filter vast product catalogues where their ranking dictates item visibility, directly driving discovery, engagement, and revenue ( Covington et al., 2016 ) . As an example, Sequential recommendation predicts the next item from ordered interactions, closely mirroring real-world deployment where user preferences evolve and recent user’s interaction history is most informative ( Rendle et al., 2010 ) . There exists essentially two paradigms for sequential recommendation, both of which learn a single conditional model of the next item. The first family encodes the history with an autoregressive sequence model and scores items against a learned embedding table, moving from recurrent ( Hidasi et al., 2016 ) and convolutional ( Tang and Wang, 2018 ) encoders to causal self-attention ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ) , backbone of later variants ( Sun et al., 2019 ; Zhou et al., 2020 ; Zhai et al., 2024 ) . The second family treats retrieval as generation ( Tay et al., 2022 ) : TIGER ( Rajput et al., 2023 ) quantizes item content embeddings into semantic identifiers and decodes the next item’s identifier token by token, which helps on rare items at the cost of a content encoder, a learned tokenizer and beam search. Both families nonetheless learn a single conditional model of the next item: one query representation, one score vector, one ranked list.

sections.heading: Next-item prediction is ambiguous.
sections.text: An user’s interaction history rarely determines the next item: it points to a set of plausible continuations, often in unrelated parts of the catalogue, so the next-item distribution is multimodal and a single query vector trained with cross-entropy settles between the modes instead of matching any one. Multi-interest learning addresses this by representing each user with several vectors, extracted by dynamic routing over capsules in MIND ( Li et al., 2019 ) , by multi-head attention with a diversity–accuracy aggregation step in ComiRec ( Cen et al., 2020 ) , or by activating a few concepts from a shared pool in SINE ( Tan et al., 2021 ) . REMI ( Xie et al., 2023 ) keeps the same architecture and instead adds interest-aware hard negatives and a regularizer against routing collapse , where all interests attend to the same historical item. These methods already rely on a form of winner-takes-all (WTA) training, but it comes with the routing architecture and WTA is rarely examined as an objective in its own right. As a result, the optimal interests are not characterized, and diversity is usually encouraged through the architecture or additional penalties.

sections.heading: Our approach: COMPOTE.
sections.text: We frame next-item prediction as an inherently ambiguous learning problem and adopt multiple-choice learning (MCL) ( Guzman-Rivera et al., 2012 ; Lee et al., 2016 ; Rupprecht et al., 2017 ) , where a model outputs M M candidate hypotheses, but optimizes only the best-performing head. While this winner-takes-all objective effectively quantizes the conditional next-item distribution ( Letzelter et al., 2024 ) , it is prone to sub-optimal local minima where heads that underperform early permanently deactivate. Annealed MCL ( Perera et al., 2024 ) mitigates this initialization sensitivity by annealing a soft-assignment temperature during training. We adapt this formulation to discrete catalogues with CO llapse-resistant M ultiple hy POT hesis l E arning (COMPOTE; Section 2 ). A shared causal transformer feeds M M prediction heads, each defining a distinct distribution over the catalogue, which are optimized via the objective function ℓ τ \ell_{\tau} in Equation 3 where τ \tau is the temperature parameter. At high temperatures, all heads update uniformly; as the temperature vanishes, the objective smoothly converges to pure winner-takes-all. For inference and retrieval, we introduce max-similarity, a normalizer-free counterpart to the loss’s max-pooling operator ( Proposition 5 ), which matches max-pooling accuracy on standard benchmarks while bypassing catalogue-wide softmax operations ( Section 4.1 ).

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: Methodologically, we propose COMPOTE, extending annealed multiple-choice learning to sequential recommendation alongside an efficient, normalizer-free retrieval rule ( Section 2 ). On the theoretical front, we first establish a generalization bound scaling logarithmically in the number of hypotheses M M ( Theorem 4 ). We further characterize the optimal hypotheses in the winner-takes-all limit, showing they partition the conditional item distribution into maximum-entropy regions ( Theorem 7 ) and that pooled hypothesis scores preserve the Bayes ranking up to saturation ties ( Proposition 6 ), proving head specialization emerges naturally without explicit diversity regularizers. Finally, across three Amazon Reviews 2023 benchmarks, COMPOTE consistently outperforms ID-based, generative, and multi-interest sequential baselines using item IDs alone, with capacity-matched ablations attributing these gains directly to the annealed MCL objective rather than model scaling, ensembling, or expert routing ( Section 4 ).

sections.text: We consider a supervised learning setting where a query 𝐱 ∈ 𝒳 {\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{X} has an associated relevant item 𝐲 {\mathbf{y}} in a catalog 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} of N N items, and the goal is to learn a model g : 𝒳 → 𝔖 N g:\mathcal{X}\to{\mathfrak{S}}_{N} mapping a query to a ranking of the items, i.e., a permutation of { 1 , … , N } \{1,\ldots,N\} . Data pairs ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) ∼ ℙ 𝐱 , 𝐲 (\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathbb{P}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} are drawn i.i.d. from an unknown underlying probability distribution over 𝒳 × 𝒴 \mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y} . In recommendation, queries are user histories and items are the entities being recommended (products, movies, etc.). We define Δ N ​ 9 ​ 1 = { 𝐩 ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] N : ‖ 𝐩 ‖ 1 = 1 } \Delta^{N\mhyphen 1}=\{\mathbf{p}\in[0,1]^{N}:\|{\mathbf{p}}\|_{1}=1\} as the ( N ​ 9 ​ 1 ) (N\mhyphen 1) -dimensional probability simplex over 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} .

sections.heading: Datasets.
sections.text: We instantiate this setting on three categories from the Amazon 2023 review corpus ( Hou et al., 2024 ) : Musical Instruments , Industrial and Scientific , and Video Games . A query 𝐱 {\mathbf{x}} is a user’s chronologically ordered interaction history, and the target 𝐲 {\mathbf{y}} is the next reviewed item. Each category contains approximately 25,000 25{,}000 items and between 50,000 50{,}000 and 95,000 95{,}000 users ( Table 5 ). Because each user contributes few observations relative to the catalog size, several next items may be plausible given the same history.

sections.heading: Learning Stabilization.
sections.text: We observe that training f f can be stabilized through the joint learning of the confidence score head via a binary cross-entropy loss over γ ^ \hat{\gamma} (see Figure 1 ). This finding aligns with the fact that the min \min operator is non-smooth and can be challenging to optimize. While beneficial, this effect is not the primary driver of the overall performance gains (see ablation study in Appendix G ). Consequently, the formalization and technical details of this stabilization term are deferred to the appendix (see Appendix H ).

sections.heading: Preprocessing and protocol.
sections.text: We evaluate on the three Amazon 2023 subsets introduced in Section 2 . Following prior work ( Rajput et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2020 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) , we apply the benchmark 5-core filtering ( Amazon Reviews’23 Benchmark, 2023 ) , which iteratively discards users and items with fewer than five interactions, and truncate histories to 50 50 items at both training and test time. We adopt the leave-one-out split of Kang and McAuley (2018) : the last interaction of each user is the test target, the penultimate one is used for validation and the remainder for training. We report Hit Rate (H@ K K ) and NDCG (N@ K K ) for K ∈ { 5 , 10 } K\in\{5,10\} , computed by ranking the entire catalog rather than sampled negatives; since each test instance has a single relevant item, H@ K K coincides with Recall@ K K .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare against seven ID-based sequential recommenders (Caser ( Tang and Wang, 2018 ) , HGN ( Ma et al., 2019 ) , GRU4Rec ( Hidasi et al., 2016 ) , BERT4Rec ( Sun et al., 2019 ) , SASRec ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ) , HSTU ( Zhai et al., 2024 ) and S3-Rec ( Zhou et al., 2020 ) ) and against the generative recommender TIGER ( Rajput et al., 2023 ) , whose numbers we take from Zheng et al. (2025) . Because COMPOTE predicts several hypotheses per query, we also compare against six multi-interest recommenders that represent a user by several vectors: MIND ( Li et al., 2019 ) , ComiRec-DR and ComiRec-SA ( Cen et al., 2020 ) , SINE ( Tan et al., 2021 ) , Re4 ( Zhang et al., 2022 ) and REMI ( Xie et al., 2023 ) , which we train ourselves under the protocol above. Appendix F describes each method. In Table 1 , COMPOTE is best in 11 11 of the 12 12 columns, the exception being H@10 on Scientific where HSTU ( 4.29 4.29 ) and TIGER ( 4.22 4.22 ) edge it out ( 4.20 4.20 ). Against TIGER, the strongest baseline on NDCG, COMPOTE improves N@5 by 9.7 % 9.7\% on Scientific and 9.6 % 9.6\% on Game, and ties on Instrument ( 2.44 → 2.45 2.44\to 2.45 ). Note that TIGER performs autoregressive generative retrieval over semantic identifiers derived from item text and decodes them with beam search at inference, while COMPOTE sees item identifiers only and ranks the catalogue in a single forward pass: modelling the multimodality of the next-item distribution suffices to beat a content-aware generative recommender.

sections.heading: 4.2 Ablations: Where Do the Gains Come From?
sections.text: COMPOTE could outperform a single-head model for three distinct reasons, additional capacity, naive ensembling, or mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing. We isolate each with a matched-capacity variant ( Table 3 ). COMPOTE outperforms all three on every dataset and metric. Not a bigger model: MCT-SASRec spends the parameter budget of COMPOTE on a single hypothesis with a deeper prediction head. It is the strongest of the three variants and still trails COMPOTE everywhere (N@5 of 2.34 2.34 against 2.45 2.45 on Instrument, 1.71 1.71 against 1.92 1.92 on Scientific, 3.78 3.78 against 4.01 4.01 on Game). At equal capacity, the multi-hypothesis parameterization beats a deeper single-hypothesis head. sections.heading: 6 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced COMPOTE, which uses annealed multiple-hypothesis learning to produce complementary rankings for sequential recommendation. Our theoretical and empirical results show that it prevents head collapse, preserves ranking quality, and improves performance across three benchmarks. We leave combining COMPOTE with semantic identifiers for future work, which could improve recommendations for rare items. It also remains to explain why its theoretically query-dependent cells form an almost static catalogue tiling and how this structure relates to item-embedding geometry ( Appendix M ).

sections.heading: Appendix F Compared Models
sections.text: We detail here the baselines summarized in Section 4 . Numbers for the sequential and generative recommenders come from Zheng et al. [2025] , who train them with RecBole [ Zhao et al., 2021 ] under a common protocol and tune them by grid search. The multi-interest models are trained by us.

sections.heading: ID-based sequential recommenders.
sections.text: 1. Caser [ Tang and Wang, 2018 ] applies horizontal and vertical convolutions to the embedded interaction sequence, capturing both positional and skip-behaviour patterns. 2. HGN [ Ma et al., 2019 ] combines feature-level and instance-level gating to modulate item embeddings according to the user representation. 3. GRU4Rec [ Hidasi et al., 2016 ] encodes the interaction sequence with gated recurrent units trained for session-based next-item prediction. 4. BERT4Rec [ Sun et al., 2019 ] uses a bidirectional transformer encoder trained with a masked-item objective, so that each position is predicted from both past and future context. 5. SASRec [ Kang and McAuley, 2018 ] uses a unidirectional (causal) self-attention encoder and predicts the next item by inner product with the item embeddings; it is the closest single-hypothesis analogue of our backbone. 6. HSTU [ Zhai et al., 2024 ] introduces hierarchical sequential transducers that consume actions and timestamps jointly, and is designed for scalability while remaining ID-based. 7. S3-Rec [ Zhou et al., 2020 ] pre-trains the sequence encoder with self-supervised objectives built from item–attribute correlations, then fine-tunes it for next-item prediction.

sections.heading: Generative recommender.
sections.text: TIGER [ Rajput et al., 2023 ] quantizes item text embeddings into semantic identifiers with an RQ-VAE and casts recommendation as autoregressive generation of the target identifier, retrieving items by beam search over the identifier space.

sections.heading: Multi-interest recommenders.
sections.text: These models represent a user by M M vectors instead of one, and are the closest existing analogue of our multi-hypothesis parameterization. We train them with the sampled-softmax objective and the readout rule of their reference implementations, and rank the catalogue by the maximum inner product over the M M interest vectors, which is the retrieval rule all of them adopt. 1. MIND [ Li et al., 2019 ] extracts interests with a dynamic-routing capsule network over the history and trains the interest whose inner product with the target is largest. 2. ComiRec [ Cen et al., 2020 ] comes in two variants: ComiRec-DR keeps the capsule routing of MIND with a bilinear mapping, while ComiRec-SA replaces it by a multi-head self-attentive pooling of the history. 3. SINE [ Tan et al., 2021 ] selects a sparse subset of concepts from a large learned concept pool, forms one interest per selected concept, and aggregates them back into a single user vector used for retrieval. 4. Re4 [ Zhang et al., 2022 ] augments ComiRec-SA with three backward-flow regularizers—contrasting interests against each other, realigning the attention with the retrieval criterion, and reconstructing the assigned items from each interest. 5. REMI [ Xie et al., 2023 ] augments ComiRec-SA with interest-aware hard-negative mining in the sampled softmax and a variance-based regularizer on the item-to-interest routing matrix that prevents routing collapse.

sections.heading: Appendix G Ablation on the Score-Loss Weight
sections.text: This appendix measures how much of the performance of COMPOTE comes from the score loss of Equation 31 , whose weight in the training objective is α \alpha ( Equation 33 ).

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: We train COMPOTE on Scientific with M = 3 M=3 for α ∈ { 0 , 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 } \alpha\in\{0,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.5,0.7\} , all other hyperparameters being fixed to the values of Section 4 . Rankings use max-similarity aggregation ( Equation 1 ), which does not read γ ^ \hat{\gamma} at inference. The score loss can therefore only change the ranking through its gradient on the shared encoder; the oracle assignments it regresses are detached from the computation graph. We report N@5 at the best checkpoint.

sections.heading: The score loss helps.
sections.text: The best weight, α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 , reaches 1.91 1.91 N@5 against 1.82 1.82 without the score loss ( Figure 4 ), and four of the six positive weights improve over α = 0 \alpha=0 . We use α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 in all other experiments.

sections.heading: It is not the main contributor.
sections.text: With α = 0 \alpha=0 , COMPOTE already outperforms every single-hypothesis variant of Table 3 on Scientific : 1.82 1.82 N@5 against 1.71 1.71 for MCT-SASRec, 1.64 1.64 for MCT-Router and 1.60 1.60 for MCT-EnsCE. The gain over single-hypothesis training is therefore obtained by the multiple-hypothesis objective alone. Moreover, the curve is not monotonic: α = 0.2 \alpha=0.2 and α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 fall below α = 0 \alpha=0 , so the effect of the score loss is of the same order as the variation across weights. The score loss acts as an auxiliary regularizer of the shared encoder rather than as the source of the improvement. Figure 4: Effect of the score-loss weight α \alpha . N@5 (%) on Scientific with M = 3 M=3 under max-similarity aggregation, as a function of the weight α \alpha of the score loss in Equation 33 . Ticks are evenly spaced and do not follow the scale of α \alpha . Without the score loss ( α = 0 \alpha=0 ), COMPOTE already reaches 1.82 1.82 , above every single-hypothesis variant of Table 3 ; the best weight α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 adds 0.09 0.09 points.

sections.heading: Appendix I Impact of the number of hypotheses M M on learning
sections.text: In Theorem 4 in Section 3 , we have established that the generalization gap between the empirical WTA loss and the expected WTA loss has a sublinear dependence on the number of hypotheses M M . We present here an empirical validation of this theoretical insight. Keeping the experimental setup used for performance evaluation described in Section 4 , we vary the number of hypotheses M M from 1 to 12 and measure the ranking quality on Scientific using N@5. Figure 5 shows that increasing M M from 1 to 3 improves ranking quality, which suggests that having multiple hypotheses is beneficial for capturing the ambiguity of the next-item distribution. However, beyond M = 3 M=3 , the performance plateaus, indicating that adding more hypotheses does not necessarily lead to better ranking quality. This empirical finding is consistent with the sublinear dependence on M M in Theorem 4 , and provides practical guidance for selecting an appropriate number of hypotheses in real-world applications. For those larger value of M M , a phenomenom we have described in Proposition 6 in Section 4 can also occur, which is the saturation of the max-similarity aggregation ω \omega . Section 4 . We have stated that this saturation can happen when at least two items have large probabilities 𝐪 a ⋆ , 𝐪 b ⋆ ≥ 1 / M {\mathbf{q}}_{a}^{\star},{\mathbf{q}}_{b}^{\star}\geq 1/M . This means that as M M increases, the probability of this saturation event increases, which can lead to a degradation of the ranking quality. Figure 5: Effect of the number of hypotheses. N@5 on Scientific under max-similarity aggregation, as a function of M M . Performance improves sharply from M = 1 M=1 to M = 3 M=3 , then plateaus: increasing M M from 3 to 12 does not degrade ranking quality, in line with the sublinear dependence on M M in Theorem 4 .

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.37005v1 [cs.LG] 27 Oct 2026 COMPOTE: Collapse-Resistant Multiple-Hypothesis Learning for Sequential Recommendation Louis Castres Saint Martin Affiliation: Criteo AI Lab, Paris, France Affiliation: Sorbonne Université, CNRS, ISIR, 75005 Paris, France Clément Calauzènes Affiliation: Criteo AI Lab, Paris, France Alain Rakotomamonjy Affiliation: Criteo AI Lab, Paris, France Patrick Gallinari Affiliation: Criteo AI Lab, Paris, France Affiliation: Sorbonne Université, CNRS, ISIR, 75005 Paris, France Abstract Next-item prediction is inherently ambiguous: a single interaction history often admits multiple plausible continuations across distinct catalogue regions. Standard sequential recommenders compress these alternatives into a single prediction, conflating user intents. We introduce CO llapse-resistant M ultiple hy POT hesis l E arning (COMPOTE), a multi-hypothesis transformer trained with an annealed objective that transitions from uniform supervision to a winner-takes-all assignment. This mechanism forces hypotheses to specialize into distinct catalogue regions, while inference relies on an efficient, normalizer-free max-similarity rule. Theoretically, we show that in the population case, the optimal solutionspartition the conditional next-item distribution according to a max-entropy quantization principle, while pooled scores preserve the Bayes-optimal ranking. We also prove a generalization bound scaling logarithmically with the number of hypotheses. Across three Amazon Reviews 2023 benchmarks, COMPOTE outperforms strong ID-based, generative, and multi-interest baselines using item IDs alone. Matched-capacity ablations confirm that performance gains stem directly from the annealed objective, preventing the head collapse observed in conventional multi-head architectures, rather than added capacity, ensembling, or routing. 1 Introduction Recommender systems filter vast product catalogues where their ranking dictates item visibility, directly driving discovery, engagement, and revenue ( Covington et al., 2016 ) . As an example, Sequential recommendation predicts the next item from ordered interactions, closely mirroring real-world deployment where user preferences evolve and recent user’s interaction history is most informative ( Rendle et al., 2010 ) . There exists essentially two paradigms for sequential recommendation, both of which learn a single conditional model of the next item. The first family encodes the history with an autoregressive sequence model and scores items against a learned embedding table, moving from recurrent ( Hidasi et al., 2016 ) and convolutional ( Tang and Wang, 2018 ) encoders to causal self-attention ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ) , backbone of later variants ( Sun et al., 2019 ; Zhou et al., 2020 ; Zhai et al., 2024 ) . The second family treats retrieval as generation ( Tay et al., 2022 ) : TIGER ( Rajput et al., 2023 ) quantizes item content embeddings into semantic identifiers and decodes the next item’s identifier token by token, which helps on rare items at the cost of a content encoder, a learned tokenizer and beam search. Both families nonetheless learn a single conditional model of the next item: one query representation, one score vector, one ranked list. Next-item prediction is ambiguous. An user’s interaction history rarely determines the next item: it points to a set of plausible continuations, often in unrelated parts of the catalogue, so the next-item distribution is multimodal and a single query vector trained with cross-entropy settles between the modes instead of matching any one. Multi-interest learning addresses this by representing each user with several vectors, extracted by dynamic routing over capsules in MIND ( Li et al., 2019 ) , by multi-head attention with a diversity–accuracy aggregation step in ComiRec ( Cen et al., 2020 ) , or by activating a few concepts from a shared pool in SINE ( Tan et al., 2021 ) . REMI ( Xie et al., 2023 ) keeps the same architecture and instead adds interest-aware hard negatives and a regularizer against routing collapse , where all interests attend to the same historical item. These methods already rely on a form of winner-takes-all (WTA) training, but it comes with the routing architecture and WTA is rarely examined as an objective in its own right. As a result, the optimal interests are not characterized, and diversity is usually encouraged through the architecture or additional penalties. Our approach: COMPOTE. We frame next-item prediction as an inherently ambiguous learning problem and adopt multiple-choice learning (MCL) ( Guzman-Rivera et al., 2012 ; Lee et al., 2016 ; Rupprecht et al., 2017 ) , where a model outputs M M candidate hypotheses, but optimizes only the best-performing head. While this winner-takes-all objective effectively quantizes the conditional next-item distribution ( Letzelter et al., 2024 ) , it is prone to sub-optimal local minima where heads that underperform early permanently deactivate. Annealed MCL ( Perera et al., 2024 ) mitigates this initialization sensitivity by annealing a soft-assignment temperature during training. We adapt this formulation to discrete catalogues with CO llapse-resistant M ultiple hy POT hesis l E arning (COMPOTE; Section 2 ). A shared causal transformer feeds M M prediction heads, each defining a distinct distribution over the catalogue, which are optimized via the objective function ℓ τ \ell_{\tau} in Equation 3 where τ \tau is the temperature parameter. At high temperatures, all heads update uniformly; as the temperature vanishes, the objective smoothly converges to pure winner-takes-all. For inference and retrieval, we introduce max-similarity, a normalizer-free counterpart to the loss’s max-pooling operator ( Proposition 5 ), which matches max-pooling accuracy on standard benchmarks while bypassing catalogue-wide softmax operations ( Section 4.1 ). Contributions. Methodologically, we propose COMPOTE, extending annealed multiple-choice learning to sequential recommendation alongside an efficient, normalizer-free retrieval rule ( Section 2 ). On the theoretical front, we first establish a generalization bound scaling logarithmically in the number of hypotheses M M ( Theorem 4 ). We further characterize the optimal hypotheses in the winner-takes-all limit, showing they partition the conditional item distribution into maximum-entropy regions ( Theorem 7 ) and that pooled hypothesis scores preserve the Bayes ranking up to saturation ties ( Proposition 6 ), proving head specialization emerges naturally without explicit diversity regularizers. Finally, across three Amazon Reviews 2023 benchmarks, COMPOTE consistently outperforms ID-based, generative, and multi-interest sequential baselines using item IDs alone, with capacity-matched ablations attributing these gains directly to the annealed MCL objective rather than model scaling, ensembling, or expert routing ( Section 4 ). 2 Problem Statement and Architecture We consider a supervised learning setting where a query 𝐱 ∈ 𝒳 {\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{X} has an associated relevant item 𝐲 {\mathbf{y}} in a catalog 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} of N N items, and the goal is to learn a model g : 𝒳 → 𝔖 N g:\mathcal{X}\to{\mathfrak{S}}_{N} mapping a query to a ranking of the items, i.e., a permutation of { 1 , … , N } \{1,\ldots,N\} .
